ideas.title: Beacon Watch
ideas.concept: A hidden-movement smuggling thriller for 2-4 players where one Smuggler secretly slips contraband past a rotating lighthouse beam while up to three Coast Guard patrols try to catch her in the light. Each round the beam disc clicks to a new zone, and being caught illuminated forces an instant reveal, so every turn is a bet on how far you can push before the light finds you.
ideas.differentiation: Hidden-movement pursuit games (Scotland Yard, Specter Ops, Fury of Dracula) reveal the hidden player on a fixed schedule (every Nth turn) or via tracking tokens; Beacon Watch instead uses a physical rotating beam disc with detented stops that the group turns each round via die roll, so the reveal trigger is a shared, tactile, semi-random rondel rather than a printed reveal-turn track. I was unable to complete live web verification this turn (WebSearch tool was unavailable/exhausted for this session), so I am not claiming this exact combination is absent from the market, only that it does not match the specific reveal mechanisms of the hidden-movement games I have direct knowledge of (Scotland Yard's fixed reveal turns, Specter Ops' tracker-chip reveal, Fury of Dracula's trail deduction). This should be re-verified with a live search before production commitment.
ideas.rules: Players: 2-4 (1 Smuggler + 1-3 Patrol). Setup: Assemble the wedge-zone coastal board (12 zones arranged in a ring around the central lighthouse peg). Mount the beam disc on the center peg, it has one lit wedge and rotates freely with 12 audible detent stops, one per zone. Smuggler takes the private tracking board (a small 12-hole peg board mirroring the public zones, hidden behind the privacy screen) and places their peg at the Harbor zone (zone 0) along with the hidden pawn. Patrol players place their 1-3 boat pawns at zone 6 (opposite the harbor). Each Patrol also gets 2 'Search' tokens. Turn structure (12 rounds max): 1) Beam Rotation: any player rolls the d12 and rotates the beam disc that many detents clockwise; whichever zone the lit wedge now covers is 'illuminated' this round. 2) Smuggler Move: secretly, on the private board, move the peg 0-2 zones along the ring (never revealing to opponents) and, once per game, load 1 of 3 contraband tokens if starting the move in the Harbor zone. 3) Reveal Check: if the Smuggler's new zone matches the illuminated zone, the Smuggler must immediately place the hidden pawn on that public zone (revealed) for this round only; it returns to hidden tracking next round unless caught. 4) Patrol Move: each Patrol boat moves 0-3 zones along the ring or across one connecting lane; if a Patrol pawn occupies the same zone as a revealed Smuggler pawn, Patrol wins immediately. Patrols may each spend one Search token per game to force an off-schedule Reveal Check on the Smuggler's actual current zone. Scoring/Win: Smuggler wins by delivering all 3 contraband tokens to the Drop Zone (zone 9) without ever being caught while revealed, or by surviving 12 rounds with at least 1 contraband delivered. Patrol wins by catching the Smuggler's revealed pawn at any point, or by preventing any delivery within 12 rounds.
ideas.components: 1 circular coastal board, PLA, 28cm diameter, 12 wedge zones printed/painted, 4mm thick. 1 rotating beam disc, PLA, 12cm diameter with cut-out lit wedge, center hole for peg mount, 12 detent notches on underside, 3mm thick. 1 center mounting peg, PLA, 5mm diameter x 15mm, press-fits into board's center hole. 1 Smuggler private tracking board, PLA, 10x10cm with 12 numbered peg holes (3mm holes) mirroring public zones. 1 smuggler pawn (hidden pawn), PLA, 2.5cm tall figure, distinct dark color. Up to 3 patrol boat pawns, PLA, 3cm tall boat-shaped minis, 3 distinct colors. 1 tracking peg, PLA, 3mm x 10mm dowel-style peg for the private board. 3 contraband tokens, PLA, 1.5cm cube chips. 2-6 Search tokens (2 per patrol player), PLA, 1cm discs. 1 privacy screen, PLA, two 12x8cm panels joined by a printed friction-hinge (snap-pivot, not living hinge), stands freestanding in a slotted base. 1 twelve-sided die (d12), PLA, 1.8cm. Storage box, PLA tray with lid, 30x30x6cm, with printed compartment dividers.
ideas.demand_case: Hidden-movement/deduction is a well-established BGG mechanism category (the 'Hidden Movement' mechanism tag covers hundreds of games including Scotland Yard, one of the best-selling family deduction games ever published, in continuous print since 1983 across multiple Ravensburger editions) with strong crossover into the broader pursuit/hidden-role genre. Target audience: family/casual groups age 10+ who enjoy light deduction and pursuit tension, 45-60 minute playtime, 2-4 players, the same audience that has sustained Scotland Yard's decades-long print run.
ideas.fun_case: The core weekly tension is a resource-management bluff: the Smuggler must weigh moving fast (risk of landing in the newly-lit zone) against moving cautiously (risk of running out of the 12-round clock). Because the beam rotates by an unpredictable die-driven amount each round rather than a fixed schedule, Patrol can't simply count down to the next reveal the way Scotland Yard players count to the next Mr. X reveal turn, keeping both sides guessing turn to turn, the same tension that makes Scotland Yard and Fury of Dracula replay well at this playtime and complexity.
ideas.producibility_notes: 12 components total, no paper anywhere. Riskiest joint: the beam disc's 12 detent stops on its underside meeting matching bumps on the board's center boss, a known, validated FDM feature (detent/click mechanisms are common in printed spinners and lazy-susan lids) but requires the detent bump height (recommend 0.8-1.2mm) to be printed cleanly, which is above the 1mm-feature risk floor and should be fine at 0.2mm layer height. The privacy screen's snap-pivot hinge is a simple two-lug press-fit rotating joint (validated joint type), not a living hinge. All pawns are single-piece prints with no assembly. Center peg is a straightforward press-fit dowel, standard FDM tolerance (0.2-0.3mm clearance).
ideas.prompt: Product photography of a board game box and contents on a wooden table: a round coastal-themed game board (deep navy blue with painted tan wedge zones and a small white lighthouse icon at center) with a rotating beam disc mounted on a center peg, one wedge cut out and painted bright yellow to represent the lighthouse beam; scattered around the board are small 3D-printed boat pawns in red, green, and orange, one dark hooded smuggler pawn figure, a small twelve-hole wooden-look private tracking board with a peg, a black twelve-sided die, tiny cube-shaped contraband tokens, and a folded two-panel privacy screen printed with a lighthouse silhouette; a matching product box behind everything shows the title 'Beacon Watch' in bold nautical lettering over a lighthouse beam graphic; warm directional lighting, shallow depth of field, muted navy-and-brass color palette.

ideas.title: Terraform Ridge
ideas.concept: A tile-laying kingdom-builder for 2-4 players where every tile is physically raised at a different elevation, and you may only extend your farmland onto a tile whose printed height sits within one level of the tile you're building from. Drafting order is set by height too, pick a low tile now for cheap early access, or gamble on a tall tile that lets you dominate the ridge later.
ideas.differentiation: Base game/mechanic: Kingdomino (Bruno Cathala, Blue Orange, 2017 Spiel des Jahres winner), flat double-sided domino tiles drafted in turn order set by tile value, placed edge-to-terrain-type-matching on a personal 5x5 grid. Specific rule-level change: Terraform Ridge tiles are physically 3D-printed with 4 distinct raised elevation levels (molded into the tile itself, not a printed number), placement legality is governed by physical elevation adjacency (within 1 printed level) instead of Kingdomino's terrain-type matching, and draft order is set by tile height rather than a printed corner number. This turns a rule that is entirely visual/printed in Kingdomino into a rule you check by touch/sight on a physical relief surface, a change enabled specifically by the 3D-print medium. I could not complete live search verification this session (WebSearch was unavailable), so treat the novelty claim as based on direct knowledge of Kingdomino's published ruleset rather than a confirmed absence of any 3D-relief tile-laying game on the market, recommend re-checking before production lock.
ideas.rules: Players: 2-4. Setup: Shuffle the 48 elevation tiles (each a 2-square domino-shaped tile, one square per tile-half, molded at a height of 1-4 printed levels per half) into a face-down stack. Reveal tiles equal to player count +1 into the draft row, ranked left-to-right by their COMBINED elevation (sum of both halves' levels, lowest to highest). Each player begins with one Castle tile (a flat, level-2 starter placed in front of them). Turn structure (draft-and-place, Kingdomino-style): On your turn, 1) place the tile you selected last round onto your personal terrain area, a new tile's placed half must sit orthogonally adjacent to an already-placed tile, and the elevation levels of the two touching halves must differ by at most 1 (you may rotate the tile in 90-degree increments to satisfy this); if you cannot legally place, discard it face down (no score). 2) Select your next tile from the current draft row (any remaining tile), this determines your turn order next round (lower combined elevation = earlier turn next round, matching Kingdomino's core drafting tension). Continue until all tiles are drawn (roughly 12 rounds for 4 players). Scoring: each connected same-terrain-type region (terrain type is color-coded, printed separately from elevation) scores (number of tiles in region) x (highest single elevation level touched anywhere in that region). Highest total score wins; ties broken by largest single region.
ideas.components: 48 domino-style elevation tiles, PLA multi-color print (color = terrain type: green farmland, blue water, brown mountain, yellow field), each tile 6x3cm, molded relief height per half ranging 3mm (level 1) to 12mm (level 4) in 3mm steps. 4 Castle starter tiles, PLA, 3x3cm, fixed level-2 height, one per player color. 1 elevation reference gauge, PLA, a small stepped ruler tile showing all 4 levels side by side for quick legality checks. 4 circular scoring dials, PLA, 6cm diameter with a rotating pointer arm on a center peg, one per player. Storage box, PLA tray with lid, 24x18x6cm, with molded tile-slot dividers by terrain color.
ideas.demand_case: Tile-laying/drafting is one of BGG's largest mechanism categories, and Kingdomino specifically is a strong demand proof point: it won the 2017 Spiel des Jahres (SdJ), the industry's highest-profile family-game award, and has sold in the multi-hundred-thousand-copies range with several expansions (Age of Giants, Origins) sustaining the line for years. Target audience: family game night, ages 8+, 15-30 minute playtime, the same buyers who already own or want Kingdomino-style light drafting games.
ideas.fun_case: The core weekly decision doubles what Kingdomino already does well (draft-order-vs-tile-value tension) with a second, tactile layer: you're now also solving a physical-adjacency puzzle by touch, deciding whether to grab a tall tile that scores big but is hard to legally connect to, or a flat one that's always placeable but low-value. Kingdomino's SdJ win and long shelf life validate that this exact 'value now vs. placement flexibility later' tension is broadly fun at family-game complexity; the elevation layer adds a genuine new sub-decision without raising the rules count much.
ideas.producibility_notes: 52 total tiles + 1 gauge + 4 dials, all single-material PLA prints, no assembly required beyond snap-peg score dials. Riskiest feature: the 3mm elevation steps between levels are printable but tight, recommend a minimum wall/step thickness of 3mm (above the 1mm risk floor) and testing that level-1 (3mm) tiles don't warp or become fragile at typical FDM infill; if warping proves an issue on a physical test print, level heights could be raised to a 4mm base with 4mm-per-level steps at zero rules cost. Score dials use a validated peg-in-hole rotating pointer, same joint as a common printed clock/spinner. No dimension anywhere is under 1mm; no glue or hardware needed.
ideas.prompt: Overhead product photograph of a tabletop kingdom-building game: a 4x4 grid of colorful raised terrain tiles on a wooden table, tiles visibly stepped in height like a topographic model, pale green flat farmland tiles, taller brown mountain tiles rising in visible 3D steps, blue water tiles at the lowest level, all in a warm matte PLA finish; a stack of unplaced domino-shaped tiles beside the grid showing their side-profile height differences clearly; four small circular scoring dials with colored pointer arms at the corners in red, blue, yellow, green; a game box behind labeled 'Terraform Ridge' with an isometric illustration of stepped colorful terrain; bright even studio lighting emphasizing the physical relief and shadows cast by the raised tiles.
ideas.cad_prompt:
Design a complete physical tabletop board game component set for 3D-printed FDM manufacture, single material PLA per part, no non-printable materials, no glue, no metal hardware. Five distinct part types:

PART 1 — Elevation Tile (domino-shaped), quantity 48 in the full set; for this build generate ONE representative instance. Overall footprint 60mm x 30mm x variable height, split into two equal 30mm x 30mm square halves joined seamlessly as one printed piece. Each half has a flat 2mm-thick base plate with a flat-topped rectangular plateau on top at one of 4 discrete elevation levels: Level 1 = 3mm plateau height, Level 2 = 6mm, Level 3 = 9mm, Level 4 = 12mm, each plateau covering the full 30x30mm half with a 1mm top-edge chamfer. This instance: left half solid green PLA at Level 2 (6mm plateau), right half solid brown PLA at Level 4 (12mm plateau).

PART 2 — Castle Starter Tile, quantity 4, one per player color (solid red, blue, yellow, green PLA). Square tile, 30mm x 30mm base with 2mm base plate, fixed Level 2 elevation (one flat 6mm plateau covering the full square), single-piece print, no assembly.

PART 3 — Elevation Reference Gauge, quantity 1, neutral grey PLA. Rectangular base 30mm x 120mm x 2mm with four adjacent 30mm x 30mm square steps rising left to right at heights 3mm, 6mm, 9mm, 12mm (matching Levels 1-4 exactly), each step top face embossed with its level number (1-4), digits 5mm tall x 1mm deep. Single-piece print.

PART 4 — Scoring Dial, quantity 4, one per player color (red, blue, yellow, green PLA). Two-part assembly: (a) a circular base disc 60mm diameter x 3mm thick with a 4mm-diameter x 4mm-tall integrated center peg, and score numbers 0-40 embossed around the outer edge in 10-point increments (3mm tall digits); (b) a separate pointer arm 25mm long x 5mm wide x 2mm thick, tapered to a point at one end, with a 4.3mm-diameter through-hole at the pivot end (0.3mm clearance around the disc's peg for a loose friction-fit rotating joint). Pointer arm snaps onto the peg after printing.

PART 5 — Storage Box, quantity 1, neutral grey/natural PLA, two-part friction-fit assembly, no hinge, no hardware: (a) base tray, external 240mm x 180mm x 60mm, wall thickness 2.5mm, with molded internal slot dividers forming 4 columns (each 32mm wide x 170mm deep x 15mm slot depth) for the 48 elevation tiles sorted by terrain color, plus one 35mm x 35mm x 15mm compartment for the 4 castle tiles and one 65mm x 125mm x 15mm compartment for the gauge and 4 scoring dials; (b) lid, a simple rectangular shell 245mm x 185mm x 10mm external, overlapping the tray's top edge by 5mm per side for a snug press-fit closure.

Deliver all 5 parts as separate, individually named CAD bodies/files in one project. No rulebook, no packaging graphics, no card components — every part above is the complete physical scope.

ideas.title: Silo Stack
ideas.concept: A push-your-luck stacking game for 2-5 players where you build a shared grain silo tower out of crop tokens each turn, deciding how many more tokens to risk adding to your section before passing the dice, the higher you stack, the more you score if the tower survives to your turn's end, but a collapse costs the stacker everything added that round.
ideas.differentiation: Base game/mechanic: Villa Paletti, a balancing tower game where players physically move architectural pieces to raise/lower a shared structure and score by piece placement/height (also comparable to Junk Art). Specific rule-level change: Silo Stack replaces Villa Paletti's 'remove a column and relocate it higher' action with a push-your-luck decision layer, on your turn you roll a d6 and must add that many crop tokens (from a pool, not from elsewhere on the tower) to a personal stacking zone before you may voluntarily stop, and if you keep rolling for bonus tokens instead of banking, a collapse forfeits only your own turn's unbanked tokens rather than ending the whole game's structure as in Villa Paletti (closer to Can't Stop's bust-and-lose-only-this-turn structure than to Villa Paletti's shared/permanent structure). I could not run live search verification this session (WebSearch unavailable), so this is based on direct knowledge of Villa Paletti's and Can't Stop's published rules rather than a confirmed market scan, recommend re-verification before production lock, particularly against dexterity/push-your-luck hybrids like Bausack.
ideas.rules: Players: 2-5. Setup: Place the circular silo base plate in the center of the table. Each player takes a personal stacking rod (a thin printed dowel that stands in one of 5 slots around the base's rim) and 15 crop tokens (small stackable interlocking discs) in their color, kept in a personal supply pile. Turn structure: On your turn, roll the d6. You must place that many crop tokens, one at a time, stacked onto your own rod (each token has a peg-and-socket connector so it stacks straight); after placing the required tokens, you may choose to STOP (banking all tokens currently on your rod as permanent score) or CONTINUE (roll again and add that many more). If at any point during your turn the shared silo assembly (all 5 rods plus their stacked tokens, connected loosely by a shared wobble-tray they all sit on) tips or any single rod's stack topples, you immediately lose every token you placed this turn only (previously banked tokens from earlier turns are safe) and your turn ends. Play passes clockwise. The game ends immediately when any player's banked total reaches 20 tokens, or after 8 full rounds, whichever comes first. Scoring/Win: each banked token is worth 1 point, plus a +3 bonus for the single tallest surviving rod at game end; highest total wins.
ideas.components: 1 circular silo base plate, PLA, 25cm diameter, with a recessed wobble-tray (a shallow printed platform on a rounded pivot boss for slight give) and 5 rod-mounting sockets. 5 stacking rods, PLA, 20cm tall, 8mm diameter dowels with a flared foot that seats in the base sockets. 75 crop tokens (15 per player x 5 colors), PLA, 2cm diameter interlocking discs with a center peg-and-socket connector so they stack straight, 0.8cm thick each. 1 six-sided die (d6), PLA, 1.6cm. 1 shared scoreboard strip, PLA, 30x4cm, with 5 player lanes of 20 notches each and 5 sliding score markers. Storage box, PLA tray with lid, 28x28x8cm, with a molded rod-holder insert.
ideas.demand_case: Dexterity/stacking games are a well-established BGG mechanism category with strong family-party crossover, Villa Paletti and Rhino Hero (balancing-tower games) and Jenga-style stacking games broadly are perennial family-night sellers with wide age-8+ appeal and short 15-25 minute playtimes, and push-your-luck (Can't Stop, Zombie Dice) is similarly one of the largest light-game mechanism categories on BGG. Target audience: family/party groups age 8+ wanting a quick, loud, tactile game for 3-6 players at a table.
ideas.fun_case: The core turn-by-turn decision is the classic push-your-luck bust curve (stop now and bank a safe but modest score, or keep rolling for a bigger stack that risks collapsing) layered onto a genuinely physical dexterity constraint, unlike a pure dice-based push-your-luck game (Can't Stop), the risk here is tactile and visible: you can see your stack wobbling before you decide whether to roll again. That combination of a proven bust-curve decision (validated by Can't Stop's decades of print) with real physical tension (validated by Villa Paletti/Rhino Hero's continued sales) is what should make each turn tense at the table.
ideas.producibility_notes: 82 total pieces (75 tokens dominate the count but are a single repeated geometry, low tooling risk). Riskiest feature: the base plate's wobble-tray pivot boss is the one component whose exact tolerance determines game feel (too stable and the tower never topples, too loose and every turn busts), recommend printing the pivot boss at a stated conservative clearance (0.4-0.5mm) as a validated rounded-pivot joint (a known FDM feature common in printed balancing toys, not a novel unvalidated mechanism), and treating the tray's small non-printed silicone contact pad as the one component needing a physical test-and-tune pass before locking dimensions, this is a tuning pass on a validated joint type, not an open question about whether the mechanism works at all. Crop token peg-socket connectors should use a snug 0.2mm press-fit, consistent across all 75 identical tokens.
ideas.prompt: Product photo of a party dexterity board game mid-play on a rustic wooden table: a round tan silo base plate with five thin vertical rods rising from it, each stacked with colorful interlocking disc-shaped crop tokens (gold, green, red, blue, orange) in uneven leaning stacks suggesting tension, one stack visibly taller than the others; a red six-sided die sits beside the base; a wooden-style scoreboard strip with five sliding markers is in the foreground; the game box behind shows the title 'Silo Stack' in bold farm-style lettering over an illustration of a wobbling grain silo; warm golden lighting, rustic farmhouse color palette of tan, red, and green, slight motion blur suggested near the tallest stack to convey the wobble.

ideas.title: Dome of Kings
ideas.concept: A two-player abstract strategy game played on a printed hemispherical dome studded with peg holes arranged in latitude rings, where you plant colored pegs to claim territory that wraps around the pole, a spatial-reasoning abstract that plays like Hex or Go but on a genuinely 3D surface where 'edges' don't exist because the board curves back on itself.
ideas.differentiation: Connection/territory abstracts (Hex, Go, TwixT, the GIPF-series) are foundational BGG abstract-strategy mechanisms, but every mainstream shipped example I have direct knowledge of uses a flat board, the dome's physical wraparound geometry (no board edge at the pole, adjacency defined by peg-hole proximity across a curved surface rather than a printed flat grid) is a distinct feature specifically enabled by FDM's ability to print a rigid 3D dome, which flat cardboard/laser-cut abstract-game manufacturing can't easily replicate. I could not run live search verification this session (WebSearch was unavailable), so I am not claiming no dome-shaped abstract game has ever existed as a novelty/travel product, only that it does not match any mainstream shipped abstract strategy game I have direct knowledge of. Recommend a live prior-art search before production lock, specifically for 'spherical Go' or 'dome peg abstract game' novelty products.
ideas.rules: Players: 2. Setup: The dome (a rigid hemisphere, flat side down, 20cm diameter) has 61 peg holes arranged in 6 latitude rings around a single pole hole at the apex, plus a ring of 12 equatorial holes forming the rim. Players take 30 pegs each (one color per player). Starting board is empty. Turn structure: on your turn, place one peg into any empty hole. Two pegs are 'connected' if they occupy holes that are adjacent along the dome's printed hole-grid (each hole has 4-6 physical neighbors depending on its ring, printed as shallow connecting grooves so adjacency is visually unambiguous). Capture rule: if you complete a fully enclosed ring of your own connected pegs around a single opponent peg (the opponent peg's every physical neighbor hole is either your color or an already-blocked empty hole with no escape reachable), remove that opponent peg from the board and keep it as a prisoner. Win condition: the game ends when neither player can find a legal empty hole adjacent to their own color that would extend a group (or by mutual agreement/30 total turns each), and the player controlling the larger connected group of pegs that includes the pole hole wins; ties go to whoever holds more prisoners.
ideas.components: 1 dome board, PLA, 20cm diameter hemisphere, flat base for stability, 61 peg holes (4mm diameter) connected by shallow printed grooves indicating adjacency, single-color print with contrasting paint-fill in the grooves for visibility. 60 pegs (30 per player), PLA, 4mm diameter x 12mm dowel pegs in two colors (e.g. black and white). 2 prisoner trays, PLA, small 6x4cm dish per player for holding captured pegs. Storage box, PLA tray with a domed recess matching the board's shape plus peg compartments, 24x24x12cm.
ideas.demand_case: Abstract connection/territory games are one of BGG's most durable hobbyist categories, Hex has been continuously analyzed and played competitively for over 70 years, and the GIPF Project (6 interlocking abstract games) has sustained a dedicated hobbyist following for two decades, showing real demand for premium physical abstract strategy objects beyond mass-market checkers/chess sets. Target audience: BGG-listed abstract-strategy hobbyists and gift buyers seeking a striking two-player 'coffee table' object game, ages 10+, 20-40 minute playtime.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is the same one that makes Go and Hex endlessly replayable, where to place a stone to extend your own territory while threatening to enclose the opponent's, but the dome's curved wraparound removes the 'corner/edge' strategic anchor points that flat Hex/Go boards provide, forcing genuinely different spatial reasoning every game since there's no fixed edge to play defensively against. That's a real complexity-appropriate twist for hobbyists already fluent in enclosure-based abstracts, validated by how much strategic depth the GIPF series wrings out of comparatively small rule changes to a similar enclosure/connection core.
ideas.producibility_notes: 62 total pieces (dome + 60 identical pegs + 2 trays), extremely low part-count and no fairness-critical joints, every peg is an identical simple press-fit dowel into a straight 4mm hole (a fully validated FDM joint at that diameter/depth). The one feature to flag: the dome's curved surface means the 61 holes must be modeled perpendicular to the local curved surface tangent (not all parallel to a flat base), a straightforward CAD operation (offset-normal hole placement) but needs to be checked in slicer preview for any hole whose print angle would need support material inside the hole itself, recommend orienting the dome with the pole at the print bed center and holes modeled radially so all holes print straight-down-accessible with no internal supports needed.

ideas.title: Current Drop
ideas.concept: A push-your-luck deep-sea dive for 2-6 players played on a vertical spiral tower instead of a flat track, you peg your diver deeper into the spiral each round chasing treasure, but every round the current wheel at the base is spun and physically rotates every diver's peg, sliding the whole group closer to the surface or trapping the boldest diver at depth.
ideas.differentiation: Base game/mechanic: Deep Sea Adventure (Goro Sasaki/Jun Sasaki, Oink Games, 2015), a push-your-luck game where divers move along a shared flat numbered track collecting treasure and must return to the sub before their shared oxygen (a die-based resource) runs out. Specific rule-level change: Current Drop replaces the flat linear track with a physically vertical spiral column of peg holes (depth is literal height on the table, not a printed number line) and adds a shared 'current wheel' at the base that every player spins once per round, rotating a printed disc that physically shifts every diver's peg position, adding a fully shared, simultaneous positional consequence that doesn't exist in Deep Sea Adventure's individually-controlled movement. I could not complete live search verification this session (WebSearch unavailable this turn), so this is based on direct knowledge of Deep Sea Adventure's published ruleset, not a confirmed market scan of every push-your-luck oxygen-diving game shipped since 2015, recommend re-verification before production lock.
ideas.rules: Players: 2-6. Setup: Stand the spiral tower (30cm tall, a helical groove wrapping 3 full turns from base to a 'Surface' cap) upright on its base disc, which is the current wheel, a rotating printed disc with 8 marked vent positions, free to spin on its center bearing peg. Each player takes a diver peg and places it at the Surface. Shared oxygen pool starts at 25 tokens in the center bowl. Turn structure (simultaneous rounds): 1) Descend phase: each player secretly decides and then reveals how many spiral steps (0-3) to move their diver peg deeper into the helix groove this round; each step deeper you stop on lets you draw 1 treasure token (drawn blind from the opaque draw box and placed on your peg's current spiral notch, visible to all) if that notch is empty. 2) Current phase: any player spins the base current wheel; wherever it stops, read the aligned vent marking (a number -2 to +2) and every diver's peg slides that many spiral steps up or down the helix simultaneously; divers can be dragged past treasure they already collected without losing it, but sliding past Surface with unspent moves ends that diver's dive for the round. 3) Oxygen phase: remove oxygen tokens from the shared pool equal to the number of players still below Surface; if the pool hits 0, any diver still below Surface loses all treasure carried and is pulled to Surface immediately. Ascend phase: a diver at Surface with any collected treasure banks it as permanent score and may choose to sit out remaining rounds or dive again next round (banked treasure is safe from future oxygen loss). Game ends when the oxygen pool is exhausted for the third time or after 10 rounds. Scoring: sum of banked treasure token values (each token printed with a value 1-5); highest total wins.
ideas.components: 1 spiral tower, PLA, 30cm tall x 10cm diameter, helical groove with 24 notch positions from base to Surface cap. 1 current wheel base, PLA, 15cm diameter rotating disc with 8 printed vent markings and a center bearing peg matching a socket in the tower's base. 6 diver pegs, PLA, 6 colors, 3mm x 15mm dowel pegs sized to sit in the helix notches. 30 treasure tokens, PLA, 1.5cm hexagonal chips printed with value pips 1-5 (color-coded by value). 1 opaque draw box, PLA, 8x8x4cm with a hand-hole and sliding cover so tokens are drawn blind. 1 shared oxygen bowl, PLA, 10cm diameter dish. 25 oxygen tokens, PLA, 1cm round discs. Storage box, PLA tray with lid, 32x16x16cm sized to stand the tower upright, with a printed cradle.
ideas.demand_case: Push-your-luck resource-management is one of BGG's largest light-game mechanism categories, and Deep Sea Adventure specifically is a strong direct comparable: an Oink Games title with sustained international popularity, multiple printings, and a compact-box design that has become a recognized entry point for the push-your-luck genre among family and gateway-hobbyist audiences. Target audience: family/gateway-hobbyist groups age 8+, 20-30 minute playtime, the same buyers drawn to Deep Sea Adventure's blend of light rules and real tension.
ideas.fun_case: The core weekly decision, how much deeper to push before the shared resource runs out, is Deep Sea Adventure's proven hook, but the shared current-wheel spin adds a genuinely new layer of shared risk that no individual player controls: even a cautious diver can get physically dragged deeper by someone else's bold dive, and a bold diver can get yanked to safety by luck. That extra shared-consequence layer, on top of an already-validated push-your-luck core, should increase table talk and shared tension (everyone watches the current spin together) beyond what the flat, individually-controlled original achieves.
ideas.producibility_notes: Component count is moderate (~65 pieces across 8 distinct part types: tower, wheel, 6 pegs, 30 tokens, draw box, bowl, 25 oxygen tokens). Riskiest joint: the current wheel's center bearing peg must spin freely under the tower's full weight, recommend a stepped-diameter peg (a wider shoulder bearing the load, a narrower pivot pin providing rotation) printed with a stated 0.3-0.4mm clearance, a validated lazy-susan-style FDM joint used in many printed spinning-base designs, not a novel mechanism. The helix groove's 24 identical notches should each be tested at a stated minimum depth (recommend 4mm) to reliably hold a peg without it working loose during a current-wheel spin. The draw box's sliding lid is a simple validated channel-slide joint.

ideas.title: Rune Forge
ideas.concept: A drafting and set-collection game for 2-4 players where every rune tile has a unique notched edge profile, and tiles from different players' forges will only physically click together into a 'sigil' if the rule combination they represent is actually legal, so instead of checking a rulebook, you feel whether your combo is valid with your hands before you commit it.
ideas.differentiation: Notch-fit spatial puzzles exist (Ubongo, jigsaw-style connection games), and physical validity-checking components exist in other forms (edge-matching mechanism games like Carcassonne's terrain-edge matching), but I have no direct knowledge of a shipped game where the notch profile itself encodes rule-legality for a drafting/set-collection scoring combo (as opposed to encoding spatial/terrain fit) — i.e. the notches aren't about whether tiles fit the board, they're about whether the specific resource combination you're assembling is a legal scoring set. I could not complete live search verification this session (WebSearch unavailable), so this claim is scoped to my direct knowledge and should be re-verified against edge-matching mechanism games broadly (Carcassonne-likes, Karuba, Ubongo) before production lock.
ideas.rules: Players: 2-4. Setup: Shuffle all 60 rune tiles (each a hexagonal tile, one of 5 elements: Fire, Water, Earth, Air, Spirit, with a unique notch profile per element cut into each of its 6 edges) into a face-down pool. Reveal 6 tiles into a shared draft row. Each player takes a personal Forge tray (a small printed frame that holds up to 5 tiles in a row). Turn structure: on your turn, draft 1 tile from the shared row into your Forge tray in any open slot, then refill the row from the pool. Sigil check: whenever you have 3 or more tiles in your Forge tray, you may attempt to physically push them together edge-to-edge; if the notches interlock and click flush (this only happens when the 3-5 tiles form one of the 12 printed 'legal sigil' combinations shown on the reference plaque, e.g. Fire-Fire-Water forms 'Steam', Earth-Air-Spirit forms 'Storm'), the sigil locks together as one fused piece; if the notches don't align, the tiles physically won't sit flush and you know immediately the combo is illegal without needing to check the rules text. Completed sigils are removed from your tray (freeing slots) and placed in your scoring pile face-up. Game ends when the draft pool is empty and no more sigils can be completed. Scoring: each completed sigil scores its printed point value (3-9 depending on rarity/tile count); leftover un-sigiled tiles in your tray at game end score 0. Highest total wins.
ideas.components: 60 hexagonal rune tiles, PLA, 5 element colors, 4cm across, each edge cut with one of 5 distinct notch profiles (element-specific tab/slot shapes) so only rule-legal adjacent pairs interlock flush. 4 personal Forge trays, PLA, one per player color, 22x6cm frame with 5 tile-sized recessed slots. 1 shared draft row tray, PLA, 30x6cm with 6 recessed slots. 1 printed sigil reference plaque, PLA, a flat 15x10cm tile with the 12 legal sigil combinations molded as small icon diagrams (language-independent). Storage box, PLA tray with lid, 26x22x6cm, with a hex-tile compartment grid.
ideas.demand_case: Drafting and set-collection are among BGG's largest mechanism categories (Sushi Go, Splendor, Azul-style games all sit in this space and are proven mass-market family/gateway sellers), and tactile/hands-on components have a documented appeal to the family and 'kids/all-ages' segment specifically because they let younger or newer players self-check legality without adult rules-arbitration. Target audience: family/gateway groups age 8+, 20-30 minute playtime, plus crossover appeal to parents/teachers wanting a game where kids can self-verify moves without asking an adult to check the rules.
ideas.fun_case: The core weekly decision is classic drafting tension (grab the tile you need before an opponent does, versus grab what's available and adapt your plan), but the tactile click-or-no-click validation turns rule-checking itself into positive feedback rather than a chore, every successful interlock is a small satisfying 'aha' moment, similar to how tactile confirmation drives replayability in spatial-fit games like Ubongo, while the underlying draft-and-collect loop is the same proven structure that makes Sushi Go and Splendor replay well at this complexity and length.
ideas.producibility_notes: 65 total pieces (60 tiles across 5 notch-profile families, low unique-geometry count since profiles repeat per element). Riskiest feature: the notch/tab interlocks must be precise enough to physically refuse illegal combinations while reliably accepting legal ones, recommend designing tabs/slots with a stated 0.3mm interference fit and validating all 5x5 notch-profile pairings on a physical test print before locking the full 60-tile geometry, since a profile pair that accidentally fits when it shouldn't (or vice versa) breaks the core mechanic; this is a tuning pass on a known joint type (male/female tab-slot, same family as puzzle-piece edges), not an unvalidated physics mechanism, so it's a bounded CAD-iteration risk rather than an open design question. No feature is under 1mm; trays are simple pocketed prints with no assembly.

ideas.title: Clockwork Court
ideas.concept: A hidden-role deduction game for 4-8 players where every player secretly holds a gear token with a unique tooth profile, and alliances can only be confirmed by physically meshing two gears together under the table to feel whether they interlock, turning the classic 'who can I trust' social deduction question into a literal, private, tactile handshake.
ideas.differentiation: Hidden-role social deduction (Werewolf/Mafia-style, The Resistance, Secret Hitler) is a huge BGG category, but every version I have direct knowledge of confirms alliances through voting, night-phase reveals, or verbal claims, none use a physical mesh-or-no-mesh tactile confirmation between two players' hidden tokens as the alliance-verification mechanism itself. I could not complete live search verification this session (WebSearch unavailable), so this claim is scoped to my direct knowledge of the major shipped titles in this space, not a full market scan, recommend re-verification, particularly against any 'secret handshake'-branded party games, before production lock.
ideas.rules: Players: 4-8. Setup: Shuffle the gear tokens (each player secretly draws 1) — gears come in two families: 'Loyalist' gears (tooth counts 8, 10, 12, mesh only with other Loyalist gears) and 'Saboteur' gears (tooth counts 9, 11, mesh only with other Saboteur gears; roughly 1/3 of players are Saboteurs, rounded down, minimum 1). No player reveals their gear or family to the group. Turn structure (rounds = number of players): each round has a Court Phase and a Gear-Check Phase. Court Phase: the current Chair player (rotates each round) publicly nominates a Project (assigns 2-3 other players to a task) based on table discussion and suspicion; all players vote yes/no on the nomination using printed vote discs (simultaneously revealed) — majority approves or rejects. Gear-Check Phase: if approved, the nominated players privately (hands under the table or behind the screen, one pair at a time) attempt to mesh gears with the Chair; a mesh (teeth interlock, felt by touch) silently confirms to the Chair alone whether that player is same-family as the Chair, but the Chair must publicly report only 'Project Success' or 'Project Failure' for the group (any single Saboteur among the nominated players can choose to force a Failure result regardless of mesh feedback). Track Project results publicly on the score board: 5 Successes banked = Loyalists win immediately; 3 Failures banked = Saboteurs win immediately. If neither threshold is hit after all rounds, Loyalists win by default (they need the clock to run out). Additional rule: once per game, any player may publicly challenge another to a 'Public Gear-Check' (mesh in full view), revealing only whether they're same-family to the whole table, at the cost of also revealing information about the challenger.
ideas.components: 8 gear tokens, PLA, 2 families (3 Loyalist tooth-count variants, 2 Saboteur tooth-count variants) each gear 4cm diameter with precision-molded teeth. 8 opaque privacy draw-boxes, PLA, 5x5x3cm each with a sliding lid, one per player, so a gear stays concealed until a private check. 1 project tracker board, PLA, 20x10cm with a Success/Failure peg track (5 success holes, 3 failure holes) and pegs. 16 vote discs (2 per player: Yes/No), PLA, 3cm discs. 1 Chair marker, PLA, 4cm token to indicate the rotating Chair role. Storage box, PLA tray with lid, 24x18x6cm with a compartment grid for gears and boxes.
ideas.demand_case: Hidden-role social deduction is one of BGG's most commercially dominant modern categories, The Resistance and its direct descendant Avalon, plus Secret Hitler (one of the highest-grossing crowdfunded card games ever, backed by tens of thousands of Kickstarter supporters), have established a large, proven audience for exactly this Chair-nominates/team-votes/hidden-saboteur structure. Target audience: party/game-night groups age 13+, 6-10 players ideal, 30-45 minute playtime, the same buyers who already own Secret Hitler or The Resistance.
ideas.fun_case: The core weekly tension is the genre's proven hook (public accusation and voting under incomplete information, validated at scale by The Resistance/Avalon/Secret Hitler's sustained popularity), with the gear-mesh mechanic adding a private, tactile information channel that creates a new layer of trust-testing: the Chair alone learns real information from a mesh-check but must decide whether to honestly report it, so bluffing now has a physical, sensory component (what did your hands actually feel?) instead of being purely verbal, which should generate more table talk and second-guessing than a verbal-only accusation game.
ideas.producibility_notes: ~26 total pieces across 4 distinct part types (gears, draw-boxes, tracker, discs). Riskiest feature: the two gear families' tooth profiles must reliably mesh within-family and reliably fail to mesh cross-family under the table by feel alone, recommend designing tooth pitch/pressure-angle differences large enough to be unambiguous by touch (e.g. a stated minimum 1.5mm difference in tooth pitch between the two families) and physically testing all gear pairs before locking geometry, since this is the core information-delivery mechanism of the game; the risk is bounded (gear meshing is a well-understood, validated mechanical joint type used in real clockwork and printed-gear hobbyist projects) so this is a tuning/validation pass on a known joint, not an open question about a novel physics mechanism. Draw-boxes use a simple validated slide-lid joint.

ideas.title: Volcano Climbers
ideas.concept: A push-your-luck dice-climbing race for 2-4 players themed as rival explorers scaling four smoldering volcano trails at once, roll and choose two dice-sum pairs to advance temporary climber pegs up the columns, bank your progress before the mountain erupts, or lose it all and start that trail over.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Can't Stop (Sid Sackson, 1978), a well-documented classic push-your-luck dice game with a long publication history across multiple licensed editions. Styling concept: full volcanic/expedition re-theme, the standard neutral numbered columns become four sculpted lava-flow trail columns molded with rising elevation contours, the neutral 'runner' markers become tiny explorer-pin pieces, and the dice/pairing rules remain mechanically identical to Can't Stop's rules with zero rule changes (three dice, pair-sum column choice, temporary vs. banked progress, bust-on-no-legal-pairs). This is disclosed as a reskin with no rule-level change, per the reskin discipline requirement, so it is scoped conservatively rather than claimed as innovative.
ideas.rules: Players: 2-4. Setup: The board has 4 trail columns (in place of Can't Stop's standard 11, simplified for a shorter physical relief-column design) numbered by achievable dice-sum ranges appropriate to the dice used (using 3 six-sided dice, sums range 2-12; the 4 physical columns here map to sum-bands 2-4, 5-7, 8-10, 11-12, with each band's track length inversely matched to its statistical likelihood, narrower bands are longer tracks). Each player has a permanent marker of their color kept off-board until banked. Turn structure: on your turn, roll all 3 dice. Split them into 2 groups using one of the possible dice-pairings (standard Can't Stop math: with 3 dice you can form 3 possible pair-sum combinations, choose one) and choose that pairing's two resulting sums to advance your temporary climber pegs (not yet permanent) on those 2 trail columns by 1 step each; if you already have temporary pegs active on 3 different columns and neither resulting sum matches one of those 3, you bust, lose all progress made this turn on temporary pegs and your turn ends. After a successful move, you may choose to STOP (converting all your temporary progress this turn into permanent banked progress on the board) or CONTINUE (roll again, same risk). Win condition: the first player to bank progress that reaches the top (eruption point) of any 3 of the 4 trail columns wins immediately.
ideas.components: 1 volcano board, PLA, 30x24cm base with 4 raised sculpted lava-trail columns molded in relief (varying track lengths per statistical band), 5mm-per-step molded notches for peg placement. 16 permanent explorer-pin pegs (4 per player color, one per column when banked), PLA, 1.5cm tall pin-shaped minis. 3 temporary climber pegs (single shared neutral set, since only the active player's temp progress is on the board at once), PLA, black, 1.5cm. 3 six-sided dice, PLA, 1.8cm each. Storage box, PLA tray with lid, 32x26x8cm, with a volcano-relief lid graphic and peg compartments.
ideas.demand_case: Can't Stop is a well-documented, decades-in-print push-your-luck classic (designed by Sid Sackson, originally published 1978, reprinted by multiple publishers over the following decades) and push-your-luck dice games broadly are one of BGG's largest light-game mechanism categories with strong family/party crossover (comparable to Zombie Dice and Farkle's continued retail presence). Target audience: family/party groups age 8+ who want a fast (15-20 minute), low-rules-overhead dice game, the same audience that has kept Can't Stop and its many themed reprints in circulation.
ideas.fun_case: The core turn-by-turn decision is entirely inherited from Can't Stop's proven bust-curve tension (push for one more roll to lock in more progress, versus banking now before a bust wipes the turn), this exact decision structure has sustained Can't Stop's popularity for decades, so the fun case rests on faithfully preserving that math while the volcano theme and sculpted relief trails add tactile/visual excitement (watching your peg climb a physically rising lava column) appropriate to a young family audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: 24 total pieces (board + 20 pegs + 3 dice + box), all simple single-piece prints. The board's 4 relief trail columns are the only complex geometry, and it's low-risk (static sculpted surface with molded notches, no moving parts, no joints at all beyond pegs sitting loosely in notches, not even a press-fit). No component under 1mm. This is the lowest-producibility-risk idea in the set precisely because it has zero new joints or mechanisms versus the original Can't Stop's already-simple physical requirements.

ideas.title: Beehive Harvest
ideas.concept: A classic sowing-and-capture Mancala game re-themed as rival beekeepers racing to fill their honeycomb stores, scoop pollen tokens from hexagonal comb cells and sow them counter-clockwise around a hexagonal hive board, landing your last token in an empty cell on your side to claim the opposite hive's stash.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Mancala (specifically the Kalah ruleset, an ancient sowing-game family with no single owned IP, in the public domain and sold under hundreds of commercial editions/themes worldwide). Styling concept: the standard 2-row-of-6-pits-plus-2-stores layout is reshaped into a hexagonal 'honeycomb' board where pits are molded as hexagonal comb cells, seeds become small resin pollen-ball tokens, and the two end stores become raised hive-mound reservoirs, a full visual/material re-theme with the Kalah ruleset unchanged. I could not complete live search verification this session (WebSearch unavailable) to confirm no bee-specific Mancala edition currently exists in the crowded marketplace of themed Mancala sets sold on Etsy/Amazon (this category is known from general knowledge to have very high thematic saturation), so this should be treated as a plausible-but-unverified styling niche, not a confirmed gap, recommend a live marketplace check before production commitment, and if a close bee-themed match is found, pivot the styling detail (e.g. to a specific art style or an added rules-variant insert) rather than abandoning the reskin slot.
ideas.rules: Players: 2. Setup: The hexagonal hive board has 2 rows of 6 small comb-cell pits (6 per player, facing each other) plus 2 larger hive-mound stores at each end (one per player, on their right). Each of the 12 comb-cells starts with 4 pollen tokens (48 total). Turn structure: on your turn, choose any one of your own 6 non-empty comb-cells, scoop out all its pollen tokens, and sow them one at a time counter-clockwise into each following cell (including your own hive-mound store, but skipping your opponent's hive-mound store entirely) until tokens run out. If your very last sown token lands in your own hive-mound store, you take another turn. If your last sown token lands in a previously-empty comb-cell on your own side, you capture that token plus all tokens in the directly opposite comb-cell, placing them all into your hive-mound store. Game ends when a player's row of 6 comb-cells is entirely empty at the start of their turn; the opposing player then sweeps all remaining tokens on their own side into their own store. Scoring/Win: whoever's hive-mound store holds more pollen tokens wins.
ideas.components: 1 hexagonal hive board, PLA, 34x18cm, 12 molded hexagonal comb-cell pits (4cm across, 1.5cm deep) plus 2 raised hive-mound store basins (8cm diameter) at each end. 48 pollen tokens, PLA, 1.2cm round beads in warm amber/gold tone with a subtle texture. Storage box, PLA tray with lid, 36x20x5cm, doubling as a travel case with a friction-fit lid.
ideas.demand_case: Mancala is one of the oldest and most widely-owned game families in the world, played across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia for centuries under dozens of regional rule variants, and modern commercial Kalah-ruleset editions are sold by numerous mainstream toy/game publishers as a staple family/educational product; it is also frequently recommended in early-childhood and math-education contexts for counting/strategy skill-building. Target audience: family and educational buyers ages 6+, 2-player, 15-20 minute playtime, including gift-buyers wanting a distinctive-looking classic game rather than a plain wooden set.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn, which pit to sow from, balancing setting up your own captures against not feeding tokens into your opponent's reachable capture zones, is Mancala/Kalah's proven multi-century hook, already validated by the game family's enormous cross-cultural longevity and its continued presence as a recommended family/educational game; the honeycomb re-theme changes nothing about that proven decision, only the tactile/visual experience of scooping and sowing round pollen tokens into hexagonal comb cells instead of generic round pits.
ideas.producibility_notes: 50 total pieces (board + 48 tokens + box), the simplest producibility profile in the set: zero moving joints, zero press-fits, tokens simply rest loosely in open pits. No feature under 1mm. The only design consideration is ensuring comb-cell pit depth (recommend 1.5cm) comfortably holds up to ~15-20 tokens during late-game sowing without overflowing, a straightforward volume calculation, not a tolerance risk.

ideas.title: Prism Duel
ideas.concept: A two-player abstract drop game played in a Connect-Four-style vertical frame, but every token is translucent colored plastic, when two different-colored tokens end up stacked in the same column slot, the light passing through visually blends into a third color, and your win condition is completing a line of that blended color, not your own.
ideas.differentiation: Base game/mechanic: Connect Four, a well-known classic gravity-drop vertical-frame connection game, standard rules are drop-a-token-in-a-column, first to connect 4 of your own color in a row wins. Specific rule-level change: Prism Duel's tokens are translucent (red and blue), the win condition is no longer 'connect 4 of your own color' but 'connect 4 slots showing the blended purple color' (achieved by either player dropping the second token into a column slot already holding the opponent's token, since a slot only shows blended color once both a red and a blue token occupy the front-to-back double-depth slot), and either player can complete either color's blend, meaning both players are racing toward a genuinely shared visual target rather than opposing individual-color targets. I could not complete live search verification this session (WebSearch unavailable), so this is based on direct knowledge of standard Connect Four rules, not a confirmed scan of the many existing Connect-Four variants and clones on the market, recommend re-verification before production lock, particularly against novelty 'color-mixing' or 'transparent token' Connect Four clones which are a plausible category to already exist.
ideas.rules: Players: 2. Setup: Stand the vertical frame (7 columns x 6 rows, each slot double-depth front-to-back so it can hold up to 2 tokens, one from each color, stacked directly behind each other) upright on its base. Each player takes 21 translucent tokens (Red or Blue). Turn structure: on your turn, drop 1 token of your color into any column with room; it falls to the lowest slot with space in that column, either landing in an empty slot (showing pure color) or landing behind/in front of an existing opposite-color token in that same row-position (a slot with 1 token already still has room for exactly 1 more of the other color, showing blended purple once both are present at the same row-column position; a slot that already holds a same-color token is full and cannot be dropped into further at that position, you must choose a different column). Win condition: the first player to complete any line of 4 (horizontal, vertical, or diagonal) of BLENDED (purple-showing) slots wins immediately, regardless of which player dropped which token into those slots. If the entire frame fills with no blended line of 4 completed, the game is a draw. Strategic note: because either player benefits from completing a blend, players must actively avoid handing the opponent the final blending token in a near-complete purple line, adding a bluff/timing layer beyond standard Connect Four's purely oppositional play.
ideas.components: 1 vertical frame, PLA printed in clear/translucent filament, 7x6 grid of double-depth column channels (each channel front-to-back holds 2 tokens), 35cm wide x 32cm tall, with a removable base slider (a printed panel that slides out to drop all tokens for replay, same mechanism as classic Connect Four). 42 tokens (21 red translucent, 21 blue translucent), PLA printed in translucent red/blue filament, 4cm diameter x 1cm thick discs sized to slide freely in the double-depth channels. 1 stand/base, PLA, holds the frame upright at a stable angle. Storage box, PLA tray with lid, 38x36x8cm.
ideas.demand_case: Gravity-drop connection games are an extremely well-known, broadly-owned classic mechanism (Connect Four is one of the best-known abstract games in the world, present in most family game collections), giving this twist an immediately-legible rule set for a very wide audience with no learning curve beyond the one new rule (blended color = shared target). Target audience: family/casual groups ages 6+ wanting a quick (5-10 minute), visually striking 2-player game, plus gift-buyers drawn to the translucent color-mixing novelty as a display-worthy object.
ideas.fun_case: The core spatial-blocking decision (where to drop to build toward a line while blocking the opponent) is Connect Four's proven, universally-understood hook, but flipping the win condition to a shared blended target changes the psychology from purely adversarial to a tense cooperate-or-sabotage dynamic, you often need the opponent's move to complete your line, so every turn carries a bluff layer ('do I help complete this blend, knowing they might scoop the win, or do I block it even though it costs us both') that standard Connect Four's zero-sum structure doesn't have, which should extend replay interest for an audience that already knows the base game well enough to want a fresh angle on it.
ideas.producibility_notes: 44 total pieces (frame + base + 42 tokens), low part-count. Riskiest feature: the double-depth channel must reliably let two stacked tokens (front token + back token) both slide independently to the bottom without jamming, recommend a stated channel depth of 2.2x token thickness (2.2cm for 1cm-thick tokens) and a width clearance of 0.5mm per token side, a direct, well-understood extension of the classic Connect Four drop-channel joint (a widely validated mechanism) rather than a new unvalidated one; the print-in-translucent-filament requirement is a material-selection note, not a geometry risk, though color consistency across a full print run should be checked against the filament supplier's batch variation. The base slider reuses Connect Four's standard validated slide-release joint.
